title: Committees
objective: After this level you can explain what committees do.
summary: Committees do lawmaking's detailed work. In Congress most bills die in committee; the rest get hearings and mark-up. In the UK, select committees also shadow each government department.

cards.headline: Want to see where laws are really made? Skip the big chamber.
cards.body: In 1885 Woodrow Wilson wrote: "Congress in session is Congress on public exhibition, whilst Congress in its committee-rooms is Congress at work." The speeches are the show. The committee room is the workshop.

cards.headline: Where bills go to wait
cards.body: No chamber can study every bill together, so each one is referred to a committee with its own area of policy, such as agriculture or education. And that's where most bills die. They're never reported out to the whole House or Senate. For a bill, getting introduced is easy. Getting out of committee is the hard part.

cards.headline: Hearings, then mark-up
cards.body: A bill that does get attention usually starts with a public hearing, where the committee hears witnesses representing different viewpoints. Then comes the mark-up session: members go through the bill and vote on amendments. Finally the committee reports the bill to the full chamber, or tables it, which ends the story. It's the line-by-line work Level 41's committee stage promised.

cards.fact: In the UK, a committee shadows every government department.
cards.context: The House of Commons has a select committee for each department, examining its spending, policies and administration. Committees can question ministers and officials in public. So committees don't only shape new laws; they also keep an eye on how government runs.

questions.prompt: In the US Congress, what happens to most bills after they are referred to committee?

options.label: They pass straight to the President
options.rationale: They would still need both chambers first.

options.label: They die there, never reported out
They are all sent to the Senate
options.rationale: Most never leave the committee at all.

questions.explanation: Most bills die in committee: they are never reported out to the whole House or Senate.

questions.prompt: What did Woodrow Wilson mean by calling Congress in its committee-rooms "Congress at work"?

options.label: Committees meet longer hours than the full chamber
options.rationale: His point was about where the real work happens.

options.label: The detailed lawmaking happens in committees
Committee members are paid more
options.rationale: Pay has nothing to do with it.

options.label: Floor debates are banned in Congress
options.rationale: Floor sessions happen; he called them a public exhibition.

questions.explanation: Wilson contrasted the public show of floor sessions with the real work done in committee rooms.

questions.prompt: A US committee's mark-up session is most like which stage of a UK bill's journey?

options.label: First reading
options.rationale: First reading is a formality with no debate or amendments.

options.label: Royal Assent
options.rationale: Royal Assent is the final approval, not detailed work.

options.label: Ping-pong between the Houses
options.rationale: Ping-pong settles disagreements between the Houses.

options.label: Committee stage, going line by line

questions.explanation: Both are where lawmakers go through the text in detail and vote on amendments.
